Let’s explore Chapter 3: Changing Habits—the Golden Rule of Habit Transformation.
Now that you understand how the habit loop works, you might be wondering—how do you actually change a habit you don’t want?
Here’s the secret: the most effective way to break an unwanted habit isn’t to eliminate it altogether. Instead, keep the same cue and reward, but swap in a new routine.
This idea, known as the golden rule of habit change, really taps into the way our brains are wired. It’s all about working with your mind, not against it.
Think about when you try to just stop a habit. The cue still shows up and the craving for that reward doesn’t just disappear. Without something new to take its place, the old behavior sneaks right back in.
So, what can you do instead? Insert a different routine that satisfies the same craving.
Let’s say you reach for a snack every time work gets stressful. The cue is stress. The routine is eating. The reward? Comfort, or maybe just a quick distraction.
To change this habit, you could try something like taking a short walk, chatting with a friend, or even listening to your favorite song when that stress hits. Cue and reward stay the same, but now the routine is healthier.
Why does this work? Because your brain still gets the reward it’s looking for—even though your actions are different. And over time, as you repeat that new routine, it starts to become automatic. The old habit slowly fades away.
It’s not always easy. You might have to experiment a bit to find a routine that really satisfies that craving. And patience is key—it can take several tries before something sticks.
You don’t have to do this alone, either. Having support from others can make all the difference. Maybe it’s a group, a buddy, or even just a community who cheers you on and helps keep you accountable. That’s why support groups work so well for people trying to quit smoking or beat tough addictions.
And here’s something else to remember—belief matters. When you believe change is possible, you’re way more likely to push through the tough spots. That belief might come from within, from encouragement by others, or from watching someone else succeed. It’s the foundation that helps you stick with it, especially when things get challenging.
So, what are the key ingredients for changing a habit?
First, keep the cue and reward the same—just focus on switching up the routine.
Next, don’t be afraid to try out different routines until you find one that really works for you.
Make sure you have some social support—people who can encourage you and keep you on track.
And finally, nurture that belief in yourself. Know that change is possible.
Changing habits isn’t a one-and-done kind of deal. It’s a process—one that takes awareness, a little trial and error, and support along the way.
But by following the golden rule of habit transformation, you can reshape your behavior and build new, positive routines that last.
